problems.description: init_db() now runs at module import time, creating a database file at the default DATABASE path as a side effect of importing app.py (before the test fixture can monkeypatch DATABASE). A lazy/guard init or explicit app factory would keep imports pure.

CAST(strftime('%s', created_at) AS INTEGER) in ORDER BY defeats any index on created_at; since created_at is stored in sortable 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' form via isoformat(sep=' '), plain ORDER BY created_at would sort correctly and the strftime cast is redundant.

The measured convention score of 0.67 reflects 9 violations, but most (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py) target files not touched by this commit's diff; only app.py/test_app.py PascalCase flags could relate to changed files, and neither defines a class in the diff — likely scanner artifacts skewing the score.

strengths: serialize_task centralizes datetime-to-ISO serialization at the API boundary, keeping internal representation consistent across POST/PUT/GET responses
Input validation rejects non-string title/status payloads with clean 400s instead of 500s
New pytest suite covers CRUD, ordering, validation, and 404 with an isolated tmp_path database
id DESC tiebreaker makes ordering deterministic for same-second inserts
DATETIME column type plus datetime objects improves type fidelity over bare TEXT
commit_reviews.summary: A solid greenfield session that adds real tests, input validation, and consistent serialization while only incurring a minor import-time side-effect smell.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-in-production' value; deployments that forget the env var get forgeable tokens. Mitigated by env override but worth enforcing in prod.
No tests added for the new auth endpoints or owner-scoped queries even though test_app.py exists; security-critical behavior is untested this session.
Inconsistent datetime handling: new token code uses timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) while create_task still uses datetime.utcnow(), which is deprecated in Python 3.12.
Comment says legacy tasks are 'kept accessible', but owner_id-scoped queries (WHERE owner_id = ?) exclude NULL-owned rows, so pre-auth tasks become invisible to every user via the API.
register() maps any sqlite3.IntegrityError to 'username already exists', which could mask unrelated constraint violations.

strengths: Owner_id scoping applied consistently at the query level across all task operations, providing defense-in-depth against cross-user data access.
Standard security practice: werkzeug password hashing and JWT with expiry instead of storing plaintext or using static tokens.
Backwards-compatible migration path (PRAGMA table_info check + ALTER TABLE) plus an index on the new foreign key column.
Clean require_auth decorator with functools.wraps that preserves route signatures, fitting the existing single-file Flask structure and type-hint conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted, convention-clean auth/ownership feature that extends the existing single-file Flask pattern with consistent owner scoping and secure credential handling, dragged down only by minor gaps (default secret, no tests, NULL-row legacy-task visibility) and pre-existing convention violations outside the touched file.

problems.description: New files introduce module-level constants that violate UPPER_CASE convention: celery_config.py's `broker_url` and `result_backend` (plus the decorated `celery_app` in tasks.py) should be BROKER_URL/RESULT_BACKEND/CELERY_APP. This matches the measured 0.67 convention score (9 violations across 5 files).

The web layer is coupled to broker availability: `send_notification_email.delay()` runs inline in the edit_task handler, so if Redis/broker is down the task is already committed but the request 500s (partial failure, no retry or compensation). The transition is persisted before the side effect is enqueued.

New dependency + worker process (Celery + Redis broker) is added to deliver an email task that currently only logs. Premature operational complexity for a stub — technical debt until real email sending lands.

Status-vocabulary mismatch risk: existing test_update_task asserts a status of "complete", but the new transition check and tests key on "completed". If the canonical stored value differs, notifications would never fire in production; the transition check depends on an exact string match.

strengths: Notification is only enqueued on an actual status transition to completed, avoiding duplicate emails on repeated requests — and this is covered by a dedicated test.
Email column added via the same idempotent PRAGMA-table_info migration pattern already used for owner_id, so existing databases upgrade safely.
Null-safe email handling: nullable column with graceful fallback to username in get_user_email.
New behavior is tested (enqueue on completion + no re-enqueue on repeat completion) using monkeypatched delay, keeping tests broker-free and fast.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-tested integration that follows the app's existing migration/controller patterns and correctly triggers notifications only on completion transitions, but adds a logging-only Celery dependency coupled inline to the request path and drifts on UPPER_CASE conventions in the new files.

problems.description: GET /tasks response contract changed from a bare list to an envelope {data, next_cursor, total} with no versioning or transitional handling; any client built in earlier sessions of the story silently breaks.
cursor validation passes cursor.isdigit() for arbitrarily long digit strings, but int(cursor) can then raise ValueError (Python int digit cap), producing an unhandled 500.

test_rate_limit_returns_retry_after hardcodes the 100/min default limit and depends on live Redis at redis://localhost:6379/2, with no in-memory fallback configured on the Limiter; the test and runtime behavior degrade if Redis is down or the default changes.
rate_limit_key re-decodes the JWT on every request, duplicating the verification require_auth already performs.

strengths: Rate limiting is a genuine cross-cutting concern matching the session theme, configured centrally with per-user/IP keying and a proper 429 + Retry-After error handler.
Keyset pagination lives in the repository (list_page_for_owner) with route-side validation; the id DESC cursor plus limit+1 next-page detection is correct and avoids offset scans.
New public methods carry type hints and snake_case naming, and RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URI uses UPPER_CASE, matching project conventions.
Tests were updated in-commit, including parameterized invalid-pagination cases and a rate-limit integration test.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped cross-cutting commit that adds per-user/IP rate limiting and correct keyset pagination while respecting existing repository/route/test patterns; the measured 0.67 convention score reflects repo-wide pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py), not anything this diff introduces.

compounding_issues: Seed's `created_at TEXT` column forced recurring ordering workarounds (DATETIME type change in S1, then `strftime` numeric casts persisted into the S4 repository layer) rather than a clean timestamp migration

Hardcoded Redis dependencies for both Celery (S3) and Flask-Limiter (S5) with no graceful-degradation fallback; environments without Redis get import/startup failures, and the rate-limit storage URI defaults to a fixed `redis://localhost:6379/2`
Notification email falls back to the username string (S3), so notifications can be dispatched to a non-address if email is absent
`datetime.utcnow()` (deprecated in py3.12) is baked into the repository `create_task` and never modernized across sessions
key_decisions: Adopting JWT bearer auth with per-owner task scoping (`owner_id`) in S2 reframed the seed as a multi-tenant API; every later session (notifications, rate-limit keying, pagination) respects this ownership boundary
Using additive `PRAGMA`-checked `ALTER TABLE` migrations (S2 owner_id, S3 email) instead of destructive resets — preserved legacy rows and made migration behavior directly testable

Extracting a `BaseRepository`/`TaskRepository`/`UserRepository` data-access layer with injected connection factory in S4, thinning `app.py` from ~250 to ~90 LOC and creating the seam S5's pagination method plugs into
Queueing notifications only on the pending→completed transition (S3) rather than on every update, preventing duplicate emails
Introducing a breaking paginated response contract `{data, next_cursor, total}` with intentional test rewrites in S5, treating the API change as a feature not a patch
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and consistently. Test coverage grew monotonically (7 → 14 → 14 → 21) with every session ending green, and the S4 refactor preserved all 14 tests unchanged, proving behavior was extracted without regression. The codebase matured from a single-file seed into a layered structure (routes → repositories → Celery tasks/config → dependency manifest) through a textbook arc: S1 stabilized the seed and added the test harness, S2 delivered the substantive feature (auth + multi-tenancy), S3 added async integration, S4 consolidated and simplified, and S5 applied cross-cutting hardening (rate limiting, pagination, ops). The only flat stretch is S4, which intentionally added no behavior — and it left the codebase measurably cleaner for S5.
story_review.summary: A near-textbook 5-session progression where auth-driven multi-tenancy in session 2 anchored every subsequent decision, an honest refactor paid off in session 5, and the code grew more capable, more layered, and better tested without any session regressing prior work.
